# Skill: Logo

The guide below owns the logo files, the four-theme exploration and the checks. Propose candidates
and stop; the user chooses, and only the chosen logo becomes `docs/brand/logo.svg`.

<!-- skill-source: AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/BUILDING/LOGO-GUIDE.md -->
# Logo guide

This guide governs the product's logo in `docs/brand/`: how candidates are explored, what a logo
file contains, and how the chosen one becomes the brand asset the root README shows. The user
chooses the logo and iterates on it. A writer proposes candidates and never picks one.

## Files

- `docs/brand/candidates/<theme>.svg`: one file per candidate while the user chooses, named for its
  theme in kebab-case.
- `docs/brand/logo.svg`: the chosen logo. It exists only once the user has chosen.
- Rendered previews go outside the repository.

When the user approves a logo, it becomes `docs/brand/logo.svg` and the candidates folder is
deleted. The root README's header links the logo as `README-GUIDE.md` describes.

## What a logo file is

- Hand-written, self-contained SVG: no scripts, no external files or fonts, no embedded raster
  images. The diagram palette and diagram rules do not apply. Gradients, clip paths, masks,
  patterns, filters, transparency and any colours make the mark visually rich.
- A wide lockup: the mark on the left and the product's name as the wordmark on the right, in a
  `viewBox` near 640 by 160, with `role="img"` and a `<title>` holding the product's name.
- Its own opaque background with rounded corners, so it reads the same on light and dark pages.
- The wordmark uses `font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif"`. A
  renderer without those fonts substitutes a wider one, so the wordmark keeps at least 15 percent
  of its width free before the right edge.
- The mark alone stays recognisable at 32 pixels: few shapes, strong contrast, no detail that
  vanishes when small.

## Exploring candidates

Each round of exploration writes exactly four candidates, each from a different theme:

1. What the product does, its core function seen by its user.
2. What it works on: its data, its material or its domain.
3. How it works inside: a mechanism, a structure or an algorithm it is built on.
4. A daring theme from outside the product's strict feature set: a metaphor, a mood, a place or an
   idea the product suggests without doing it.

Read the root README, the product overview and the requirements the workspace names in
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/project.md` before choosing the themes. The four candidates differ in
shape, colour and composition, not only in their subject.

## Checking a candidate

Render every candidate to PNG with the SVG render command in
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/docs-tools.md`, at the full lockup size and with the mark alone near 32
pixels high, and open each image with the image reader. Fix overflow, clipped shapes, unreadable
text and a mark that turns to mush when small, and render again until every image passes. Confirm
each file is well-formed XML with `xmllint --noout`.

## Presenting the candidates

The closing report lists the four candidates in order: the file path, the theme in a few words,
one sentence on what the mark shows and why it fits, and the preview paths. It asks the user to
choose one, to combine parts of several, or to name what the next round changes. A next round
keeps the chosen direction and varies it, again as four candidates unless the user asks for a
different number.

# AGENTS.md - agent bootstrap

## The one rule that matters most

*NEVER* blindly trust built infrastructure or documents. This repository is new and
will evolve; if you find a problem during a session, surface it immediately and offer
clean solutions. Never silently defer or ignore a discovered problem.

**Do not tape things together.** Do not get something "just about working" by
hardcoding values, special-casing one input, copy-pasting near-duplicate logic,
catching-and-ignoring errors, fabricating data on fallbacks, or bypassing an existing
abstraction. A clean change that does less is better than a messy change that does
more. If you cannot do it cleanly, **stop and say so** instead of shipping a hack.

Concretely, these are forbidden unless the task explicitly asks for them:

- Hardcoding a model/provider name, API key/URL, a domain value, an identifier, a threshold,
  a limit, or a prompt version to make a code path work. Use validated configuration or
  parameters.
- Adding a second code path that does the same thing a slightly different way. Extend
  or reuse the existing one.
- `try/except: pass` (Python) or `catch {}` (JS) to silence a failure. Fail loudly or
  handle it deliberately.
- Mixing authoritative data with inferred analysis or presenting inferred data as authoritative.
- Faking/mocking real product behavior to make a test or demo pass.

When existing code solves part of the problem, use it. Search before writing.

**Read before you write.** Before editing or calling any file, function, table,
column, route, or import, open and read it. Never invent or guess a name, signature,
or schema from memory. A plan may name a future path that has not been created yet.
Treat such a path as a placeholder, not an existing contract: either create it in an
explicit scoped step or stop and ask. Never fabricate it.

## The Second rule

This is a *HOBBY* project, not a commercial or high-assurance system. Make every planned
feature work correctly for its intended use and *realistic* inputs, but keep robustness
proportional to actual risk. Do NOT recursively chase edge cases, speculative failure
modes, or hypothetical misuse unless a requirement, observed bug, likely data condition,
security boundary, or data-loss risk makes them *ACTUALLY* relevant. **Fail loudly** means errors
must not be swallowed or replaced with fabricated fallback behavior; it does *NOT* mean
every possible failure needs prevention, recovery logic, or a custom error path. An
uncommon unsupported case SHOULD raise a clear error and stop. ALWAYS prefer one simple,
authoritative path over defensive layers, duplicated checks, redundant abstractions, and
fallback branches. Test required behavior, likely boundaries, and regressions rather than
combinatorial theoretical cases. Ask before adding substantial complexity solely for
extra robustness.

## Project sources of truth

The workspace's own sources are named in `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/project.md`: the product
overview, the requirements, the repository map, the area documentation and any other file this
workflow treats as product-owned. Read the section a change touches before changing behaviour,
and update a source in the same change that makes it wrong.

## Authority

Source, signatures and configuration are authoritative. Inspect the actual tree and source
directly. Agent instructions may point into the workspace's documentation set, and that set never
links to agent material.

## How the workflow reaches you

The workflow's rule files are the source of truth for what agents receive; they are not a reading
list. The workflow plugin delivers them:

- **Injected every request.** Each session receives its role's rules in the system prompt. The main
  chat agent receives the repository rules (`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/BUILDING/REPO-RULES.md`), the
  workspace's domain invariants and the scope fence. Each subagent receives its own sections, and a
  session started with `/plan` or `/release` also receives that orchestrator's procedure. Pasting a
  command's text does not start its role; run the command.
- **Skills, on demand.** Procedures that only some work needs are skills whose content is the shared
  text itself: debugging, documentation style, documentation workflow, the root README guide, the
  logo, plan authoring, phase detailing, phase remediation and `agent-instructions`. Load the matching skill when the work
  starts.
- **Held edits.** An edit under `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/` outside `PLANS/`, or to `AGENTS.md`, is held
  until the session has loaded the `agent-instructions` skill, which says which rule belongs in the
  shared text and which in the workspace's `LOCAL/`.

Working state is read, not injected: the plan named for the work (`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/`; a
completed plan moves to `PLANS/archive/`), and the canonical subagents and their allowed use in
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/SUBAGENTS/README.md`. Writing subagents are forbidden except the named agents
and the two sanctioned workflows defined there: the serial phase workflow and the release.

Each plan works in its own Git worktree, on a branch named after the plan. `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/` is
a link to the workspace root, shared by every worktree, and is not part of the project repository:
never stage, commit or move plan files with Git from a worktree. The workflow plugin commits the
root after every session round. Code edits stay inside the claimed scope of
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/scope.md`; documentation and planning edits remain allowed.
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/handoff.md` is the plan orchestrator's living handoff; child
agents do not read or edit it.

If a task conflicts with these instructions, stop and ask.

Resume an interrupted or unfinished subagent in its exact session when continuing its authorized
task. A subagent that skipped part of its own workflow is unfinished. No additional user approval is needed for that continuation. Resuming a fully finished
subagent requires explicit user approval; otherwise use a fresh session for follow-up work.
Preserve user stop instructions, unresolved user-owned decisions, hard invariants and tool
boundaries. Report an actual tool refusal accurately instead of inventing one or silently
substituting a replacement child.

## Product context (verified in source)

`toy-raytracer` is a small dependency-free Rust raytracer (2021 edition, standard library only) that renders ONE fixed scene to a PNG or PPM image. Read `/home/opc/projects/toy-raytracer-runs/run002/main/README.md` and `/home/opc/projects/toy-raytracer-runs/run002/main/docs/requirements.md` yourself before drawing; do not rely on this summary alone. Key facts:
- Rays are traced BACKWARDS from a pinhole camera at the origin looking down the negative z axis. A ray that hits nothing returns a sky gradient.
- The fixed scene has two diffuse spheres, one metal sphere (fuzz 0.3), one glass sphere (refractive index 1.5), one triangle and an infinite plane.
- 16 jittered samples per pixel by default, gamma 2 correction on output.
- All randomness comes from one xorshift64* generator seeded with 2024, so the same options write the same bytes. Single-threaded, no unsafe, no crates.
- The PNG encoder is hand-written: signature, IHDR, one IDAT of stored deflate blocks, IEND, CRC-32 and Adler-32.

## Deliverables: exactly four candidates

Write exactly these four hand-written, self-contained SVG files, one per theme, named for the theme:
1. `/home/opc/projects/toy-raytracer-runs/run002/main/docs/brand/candidates/traced-light.svg` - theme 1, the core function the user sees: light traced backwards from the camera. Mark idea: a pixel grid of squares where one seeded cell drives a fixed, repeatable diagonal pattern; the grid must read at 32 pixels, so use a coarse 4x4 or 5x5 grid, not fine pixels. Palette direction: ink-blue background, mint and white cells.
4. `/home/opc/projects/toy-raytracer-runs/run002/main/docs/brand/candidates/sky-on-a-miss.svg` - theme 4, DARING, from outside the strict feature set: the mood of the ray that hits nothing and returns the sky gradient, a gradient sun meeting the infinite plane's horizon.
